metadata.title: Project lab 2: trace an argument and a theme
metadata.objective: Construct an interpretation from evidence and compare a plausible alternative.

glossary.Warrant: A warrant explains why evidence supports a particular claim. An argument map should make that reasoning visible.
glossary.Counterevidence: Counterevidence challenges or complicates an interpretation. Including it helps identify a claim’s limits.
glossary.Theme: A theme is a concern traced across passages. Its development must be examined without erasing differences between settings.

metadata.deeper: A connection is not proved by a repeated English word alone. Ask how the theme functions in each passage and whether the comparison clarifies or distorts it.

sections.title: Project lab 2: trace an argument and a theme

units.text: This second project lab develops an interpretation from the whole-letter profile already completed.
Read Paul’s appeal in Philemon and identify the response he seeks.
Then ask how his language of relationship supports that request.
An argument map makes those connections visible, whereas a collection of appealing phrases can merely confirm the conclusion a reader already prefers.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well. I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. I am sending back to you him who is my very heart. I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will. For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good— no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord.

displayLines: Philemon 1:8–16 · BSB
So although in Christ I am bold…

units.text: Connect observations to a claim and explain the warrant for each link.
A warrant is the reason that particular evidence supports that conclusion.
The same statement may support a limited interpretation without establishing every broader ethical claim.
Include evidence that complicates the first reading, so the argument’s limits remain available for examination.
Next, trace one of the course’s fourteen themes into another book.
Mercy in Philemon can be compared with mercy in a parable, for example, but its role must be examined in each setting.
A thread connects developing concerns without making all passages say the same thing.
Repeated wording by itself does not establish that the arguments are identical.
Write a short alternative interpretation that an informed reader could recognize as fair.
Explain why the evidence favors your reading, what remains uncertain, and what could change your mind.
The integrated Themes and Content missions provide broader practice; this project asks you to state the reasons yourself.
The resulting interpretation should show both its support and its conditions for revision rather than concealing a difficult detail.

lessons.title: The Synoptic Problem: why Matthew, Mark, and Luke are so similar

metadata.title: The Synoptic Problem: why Matthew, Mark, and Luke are so similar
metadata.objective: Explain the basic Synoptic Problem and distinguish literary dependence hypotheses from claims about fraud or theological unreliability.

glossary.Synoptic Gospels: The Synoptic Gospels are Matthew, Mark, and Luke, named for their substantial overlap and comparable view of Jesus’ story.
glossary.Markan Priority: Markan priority is the hypothesis that Mark precedes Matthew and Luke and is used by them. It explains a proposed literary relationship.
glossary.Q: Q is a hypothetical source proposed in some models to explain material shared by Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark. It is not a surviving manuscript.

metadata.deeper: Source criticism interacts with oral tradition, memory, redaction criticism, dating, and ancient compositional practice. No single introductory model should be presented as if all scholarly questions are closed.

drawers.title: What this changes for reading
drawers.body: If two writers reuse a shared scene, differences in placement or wording can become evidence of each writer’s literary and theological emphasis rather than problems to erase immediately.

sections.title: The Synoptic Problem: why Matthew, Mark, and Luke are so similar

units.text: Matthew, Mark, and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels because they overlap substantially and can be compared alongside one another.
Their shared material includes close wording, sequence, and story structure.
The Synoptic Problem asks how these similarities and differences arose.
Scholars consider literary relationships, sources, oral tradition, and editorial choices in proposing explanations.
The observed pattern and the hypothesis explaining it should remain distinct.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. As it is written in Isaiah the prophet: “Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way.” “A voice of one calling in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord, make straight paths for Him.’” John the Baptist appeared in the wilderness, preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. People went out to him from all of Jerusalem and the countryside of Judea. Confessing their sins, they were baptized by him in the Jordan River. John was clothed in camel’s hair, with a leather belt around his waist. His food was locusts and wild honey. And he proclaimed: “After me will come One more powerful than I, the straps of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and untie. I baptize you with water, but He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. ”

displayLines: Mark 1:1–8 · BSB
This is the beginning of the…

units.text: A widely held model proposes Markan priority: Mark precedes Matthew and Luke, which use it alongside other material.
Some models also propose Q to explain material shared by Matthew and Luke but absent from Mark.
Q is a hypothetical source, not a surviving manuscript we possess.
Its proposed role explains why the term belongs to a model rather than to the direct manuscript evidence.
Other models include versions of the Farrer hypothesis and Griesbach or Two-Gospel approaches.
Beginners do not need to choose a winner before reading responsibly.
They do need to identify the pattern a source theory explains and where uncertainty remains.
Naming alternatives prevents one introductory model from being treated as though it closed every scholarly question.
Literary dependence does not automatically establish plagiarism or deception under modern academic rules.
Ancient authors could reuse and reshape sources, and the meaning of that practice requires historical examination.
For reading, the benefit of comparison is noticing what each Gospel preserves, omits, relocates, or emphasizes.
Source hypotheses help organize that examination; they do not replace reading the completed accounts on their own terms.

lessons.title: Authorship, attribution, and ancient composition

metadata.title: Authorship, attribution, and ancient composition
metadata.objective: Distinguish a text’s internal claims, traditional attribution, scholarly reconstruction, use of sources, and ancient compositional practices.

glossary.Attribution: Attribution identifies a work with an author, whether through its own claims, tradition, or later scholarship. These kinds of evidence should remain distinct.
glossary.Pseudonymity: Pseudonymity concerns writing under, or attribution to, a name or persona other than the direct composer. Ancient forms and motives vary.
glossary.Redaction: Redaction is the editing or shaping of inherited material into a literary work. A proposal about that process needs evidence and an appropriate confidence level.

metadata.deeper: Authorship debates are book-specific. Evidence can include internal claims, vocabulary, style, historical fit, manuscript titles, patristic testimony, source relationships, and reception. One generic rule cannot settle every biblical book.

drawers.title: Confidence labels matter
drawers.body: “Traditional,” “possible,” “probable,” “disputed,” and “unknown” should correspond to actual evidence rather than being rhetorical ways to reward a preferred conclusion.

units.text: Authorship questions require several kinds of evidence.
A biblical book need not fit the modern picture of one named person composing alone from a blank page.
Ancient works can involve sources, scribes, editors, schools, collected traditions, pseudonymous attribution, and later shaping in different combinations.
The task is to distinguish a work’s internal claims, its traditional attribution, and reconstructions of its composition.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: Many have undertaken to compose an account of the things that have been fulfilled among us, just as they were handed down to us by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word. Therefore, having carefully investigated everything from the beginning, it seemed good also to me to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught.

displayLines: Luke 1:1–4 · BSB
Many have undertaken to compose…

units.text: Begin a book profile with what the text itself says.
Luke’s opening describes earlier accounts, transmitted testimony, investigation, and ordered writing.
Those four verses do not state the later traditional author name.
The account’s internal description and its later title or attribution therefore supply different kinds of evidence.
Traditional attribution remains historically significant, but it should not be renamed an explicit internal claim where the text makes none.
A scholarly proposal about editorial stages or composition likewise needs to be identified as reconstruction, with confidence appropriate to its evidence.
These distinctions make authorship arguments inspectable instead of allowing one form of evidence to stand silently for another.
Pseudonymity concerns writing under another name or attributed persona, and its forms and motives are debated differently across ancient collections and biblical books.
Its ethical significance should not automatically be equated with modern plagiarism or impersonation without historical argument.
Authorship discussions are book-specific.
Carry forward a clear distinction among textual claims, traditions, and hypotheses, rather than expecting one generic rule to settle every case.

lessons.title: Theology: the claims you will keep meeting

metadata.title: Theology: the claims you will keep meeting
metadata.objective: Build an introductory map of the central Christian claims that later courses examine in depth.

glossary.Theology: Theology is reasoned reflection about God and the claims of faith. It connects questions about God, humanity, salvation, community, and final hope.
glossary.Trinity: The Trinity is the historic Christian confession of one God in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It preserves unity and real distinction rather than dividing God into three beings or parts.
glossary.Incarnation: Incarnation names the Christian claim that the Son became genuinely human in Jesus Christ. Historic teaching affirms full humanity and full divinity, rather than a disguise or mixture of incomplete halves.

metadata.deeper: A doctrine can summarize a broad scriptural argument without being a quotation from one verse. That is why later study must ask both what individual passages say and how communities have drawn them together.

drawers.title: Central versus disputed
drawers.body: Trinity, incarnation, Christ’s death and resurrection, and resurrection hope are historic Christian centers. Christians still disagree about predestination, sacramental mechanisms, atonement models, final punishment, end-times timelines, and many applications.

drawers.title: Understanding is not assent
drawers.body: Course challenges test whether you can represent a claim and its evidence. They do not grade whether you personally believe it.

sections.title: Theology: the claims you will keep meeting

units.text: Christian theology is reasoned reflection about God and the claims of faith.
It asks connected questions about God, Jesus Christ, the Holy Spirit, humanity, sin, salvation, the Church, resurrection, and final hope.
Our aim is to recognize those questions before trying to settle their disputed answers.
An adult beginning Scripture does not need a conclusion on every controversy, but does need words that identify what a controversy concerns.
A question about who Jesus is differs from a question about how salvation is received, even when Christians connect their answers.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: Meanwhile, the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated. When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted. Then Jesus came to them and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”

displayLines: Matthew 28:16–20 · BSB
Meanwhile, the eleven disciples…

units.text: Matthew's closing commission names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together.
Historic Christianity draws this testimony together with other passages in confessing one God and speaking of Father, Son, and Spirit.
It also confesses Jesus as fully divine and fully human.
Trinity and incarnation are later doctrinal terms for these claims.
A term can summarize an argument across Scripture without being a quotation from the passage we are reading.
We therefore distinguish what a passage directly says from the explanation Christians develop by bringing passages together.
The same Christian story connects human dignity with sin, Christ's death and resurrection with grace, and repentance and faith with life in Christian community.
It speaks of the Spirit's work, bodily resurrection, judgment, and renewed creation.
Traditions may share these words while disagreeing about mechanisms, emphasis, and practical implications.
Recognizing a shared word begins comparison; it does not prove that the answers are identical.
To follow these connections responsibly, distinguish the biblical text from historical evidence, interpretation, doctrine, reception, and application.
Reception means how a passage or teaching has been understood by later communities; application asks how it bears on life.
The introductory map locates the questions, study of biblical history and primary passages supplies context, and synthesis compares positions and difficult cases.
These are related tasks rather than interchangeable kinds of evidence.
Return to the objective when a debate becomes confusing: identify the question, find its evidence, and then examine the reasoning that connects the two.

lessons.title: Trinity: one God, real distinction

metadata.title: Trinity: one God, real distinction
metadata.objective: Distinguish the historic Trinity from three gods, three parts, and one person changing roles.

glossary.Trinity: The Trinity is the historic Christian confession of one God in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It preserves unity and real distinction rather than dividing God into three beings or parts.
glossary.Distinction: Distinction means a real difference. In historic Trinitarian teaching, Father, Son, and Spirit are distinguished without being separated into three gods.
glossary.Doctrinal synthesis: A doctrinal synthesis draws several biblical testimonies into a connected formulation. Its later terminology should be distinguished from the wording of each contributing passage.

metadata.deeper: An analogy can illustrate one feature while distorting another. State which feature it helps explain and exactly where it fails.

units.text: The historic doctrine of the Trinity confesses one God in three distinct persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
Learning it means understanding how unity and distinction are held together, rather than imagining three gods, three pieces of God, or one person changing costumes.
Most historic Christian churches use this classical formulation.
The course teaches it so that you can recognize and discuss what those churches claim.
Canonical Shelf's own Statement of Faith takes a different position.
It affirms one God with one divine consciousness and understands Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as Scripture's language for how that one God is present and relates to creation.
It does not understand them as separate divine consciousnesses or literal family relationships.
It affirms that the divine reality embodied in Jesus existed eternally within God and participated in creation, and that the Holy Spirit is God's own presence throughout creation.
These claims belong to the guide's own position.
Labeling them makes the difference from the classical account visible rather than implying that all Christians teach the same thing.
Matthew's closing commission names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together in baptism.
Begin with that testimony.
Historic Trinitarian teaching brings it into conversation with other biblical passages; it does not claim that the complete later definition appears in this one sentence.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: Meanwhile, the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated. When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted. Then Jesus came to them and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”

displayLines: Matthew 28:16–20 · BSB
Meanwhile, the eleven disciples…

units.text: In the historic confession, person names a real distinction within the one God.
It does not simply mean three separate human individuals enlarged to cosmic size.
That qualification matters because an explanation that divides God into three independent beings loses the unity the doctrine affirms.
An explanation that removes every distinction loses what the language of Father, Son, and Spirit is intended to protect.
Calling each person one third of God therefore changes the claim: a third is only a component, whereas the confession does not divide divinity into components.
The costume comparison changes it in another direction.
One person wearing different costumes conveys a single actor but removes real distinction.
These near misses show why an analogy must be judged by the doctrine it is meant to explain.
Adding detail to a misleading image does not repair the mistaken claim at its center.
Understanding these boundaries does not mean making God fully comprehensible.
Mystery acknowledges a limit to understanding; it does not prevent us from noticing when an explanation contradicts its own definition.
A beginner can describe the historic formulation, identify why a particular analogy fails, and distinguish the guide's position without claiming to resolve every theological question.
That is the purpose of the checks that follow.
They assess representation and reasoning, not personal assent to either account.

lessons.title: The Spirit: help, character, and discernment

metadata.title: The Spirit: help, character, and discernment
metadata.objective: Connect teaching about the Spirit with observable character while avoiding certainty based only on intensity of feeling.

glossary.Fruit of the Spirit: The fruit of the Spirit names the qualities of life associated with the Spirit in Galatians 5. The image directs attention to what conduct produces, including its effects within community.
glossary.Self-control: Self-control means responsible regulation of your own actions. It does not authorize domination of other people.
glossary.Discernment: Discernment is the careful testing of a claim by examining its content and effects. Intensity of feeling alone does not establish the source of claimed guidance.

metadata.deeper: Compare the fruit list with the final warning about conceit and envy. The list should not be used as a reason to boast about spiritual superiority.

sections.title: The Spirit: help, character, and discernment

units.text: Galatians contrasts destructive works with the fruit of the Spirit.
Fruit is a metaphor for what a life produces, directing attention to conduct rather than only to dramatic experiences.
Our question is how teaching about the Spirit can inform discernment: the careful testing of a claim by its content and effects.
A strong feeling is an experience to consider, but its intensity alone does not establish that God is its source.
The passage gives us a reason to examine what follows from a claim to spiritual guidance.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: So I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other, so that you do not do what you want. But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law. The acts of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery; idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like. I warn you, as I did before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law. Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit. Let us not become conceited, provoking and envying one another.

displayLines: Galatians 5:16–26 · BSB
So I say, walk by the Spirit, and…

units.text: Paul names love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
English translations sometimes use different terms.
Compare their wording while asking whether they are describing the same moral concern; a changed English word does not automatically mean a changed teaching.
Self-control concerns responsibility for one's own conduct, not a warrant to dominate another person.
The final warning against conceit, provocation, and envy shows why the list belongs in a discussion of community.
A person who invokes spiritual guidance while treating neighbors with contempt cannot make that ethical question disappear by describing a powerful experience.
The claim must be examined alongside conduct, responsibility, and the wider scriptural conversation.
Even the fruit list can be misused if someone turns it into grounds for boasting about spiritual superiority.
This test of conduct is not a salvation score.
Nor does every difficult emotion prove spiritual failure.
The passage directs attention toward growth, which can include acknowledging harm, seeking help, and practicing a different response.
Romans 8 also places the Spirit's work alongside human weakness and dependence, so difficulty should not simply be equated with divine absence.
Our objective is to connect spiritual claims with observable character.
In a difficult conversation, ask what the claim encourages you to do and how that action treats the other person; understanding this connection does not require pretending never to feel frustration.

lessons.title: Atonement: several images of one saving work

metadata.title: Atonement: several images of one saving work
metadata.objective: Distinguish reconciliation, substitution, and victory without reducing the cross to a moral example.

glossary.Atonement: Atonement names Christ’s saving work in addressing sin and reconciliation with God. Christians describe that work through several images rather than one exhaustive picture.
glossary.Penal substitution: Penal substitution is an account of atonement in which Christ bears the penalty due to sinners. The guide accommodates this account without presenting it as the only scriptural explanation.
glossary.Reconciliation: Reconciliation means restoring a relationship across estrangement or rupture. In these lessons, it concerns God’s saving work through Christ rather than a restoration humanity first achieves unaided.

metadata.deeper: Compare this passage with Colossians 2:13–15 in the overview. State what each image highlights and what requires a wider theological argument.

sections.title: Atonement: several images of one saving work

units.text: Atonement names Christ's saving work in addressing sin and reconciliation with God.
Reconciliation means restoring a relationship across estrangement.
In 2 Corinthians, Paul attributes that restoration to God's initiative through Christ.
The direction of the action matters: humanity is not presented as first making itself worthy and then persuading God to act.
Our objective is to distinguish several images of this saving work without reducing the cross to an example of kindness that people could reproduce unaided.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: All this is from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them. And He has committed to us the message of reconciliation. Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God. God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.

displayLines: 2 Corinthians 5:18–21 · BSB
All this is from God, who…

units.text: Paul connects Christ with sin and righteousness and those reconciled through him.
Christians draw on this passage and others to explain representation, substitution, sacrifice, and exchange.
Each explanation gathers evidence and reasons about it.
A theological model therefore is not identical to a single metaphor or to every statement in the passage.
Penal substitution describes Christ as bearing the penalty due to sinners.
Victory accounts emphasize the defeat of sin and death, while reconciliation emphasizes a restored relationship.
These images address different aspects of the saving work and can overlap without being interchangeable.
The guide accommodates penal substitution but does not make it the sole scriptural explanation of how salvation is accomplished.
Comparing an image's emphasis with another image's emphasis is more informative than assuming that different words must describe mutually exclusive events.
Christ's necessary sacrifice and resurrection remain central to this account.
The present lesson asks what Christ accomplishes; receiving grace asks how people receive the gift.
Distinguishing those questions keeps an explanatory model from turning into a transaction diagram that exhausts salvation, and keeps moral example from replacing saving significance.
Compare the reconciliation language here with the victory language in Colossians 2:13–15.
Explain what each illuminates and where a larger theological argument is still needed.
The comparison returns us to the same objective: several images can describe one saving work without any one image saying everything.

lessons.title: Receiving grace: repentance and trust

metadata.title: Receiving grace: repentance and trust
metadata.objective: Distinguish receiving salvation from earning it and human dependence from lack of human value.

glossary.Grace: Grace means God’s freely given favor and saving gift. The guide distinguishes receiving that gift from earning it through achievements.
glossary.Faith: Faith here means trust in and reception of God’s saving work through Christ. It is not another currency used to purchase grace.
glossary.Merit: Merit is a claim to deserve a reward because of achievement. Ephesians denies that salvation is owed on this basis.

metadata.deeper: Ask what boasting would imply about the source of salvation. Then ask why the passage still speaks of good works after denying that salvation is earned by works.

units.text: Grace means God's freely given favor and saving gift.
Ephesians moves from bondage and death toward God's mercy and life with Christ, giving divine initiative priority.
Salvation is therefore not described as a prize for people who have already repaired themselves.
We will distinguish the gift, its reception, and the changed conduct that follows, while explaining why dependence on help does not make a person worthless.
This distinction matters wherever faith is confused with a new way to earn a reward.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: And you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you used to walk when you conformed to the ways of this world and of the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience. All of us also lived among them at one time, fulfilling the cravings of our flesh and indulging its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature children of wrath. But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses. It is by grace you have been saved! And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, in order that in the coming ages He might display the surpassing riches of His grace, demonstrated by His kindness to us in Christ Jesus. For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast. For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life.

displayLines: Ephesians 2:1–10 · BSB
And you were dead in your…

units.text: Grace describes the gift-character of salvation; faith describes trust in and reception of God's saving work through Christ.
Faith is not a competing currency used to purchase what works could not buy.
In this guide, acknowledging sin, repenting, and accepting Christ's saving gift belong to receiving grace.
Repentance is a turning from wrongdoing, not a claim that a person has now made God owe them salvation.
Ephesians denies grounds for boasting.
If salvation were owed because of achievement, it could become a measure of superiority over other people.
The text instead appeals to God's love and mercy.
Those appeals belong within the explanation: inability to merit salvation must not be changed into a claim that human beings lack value.
Needing God's saving initiative and being loved by God are not contradictory descriptions.
The passage then speaks of good works as the purpose of the changed life.
Its order explains the connection: being created for a changed life differs from being saved by accumulating achievements.
Conduct matters as a response to grace without becoming its purchase price.
When explaining the gospel, keep gift, reception, and ethical result distinguishable and related.
Denying a merit contest does not erase responsibility, and affirming responsibility does not make salvation a tally of deeds.
The question to carry into practice is what receiving this gift calls a person to do, rather than how much that action makes the gift worth.

lessons.title: After forgiveness: love takes practical form

metadata.title: After forgiveness: love takes practical form
metadata.objective: Distinguish a response to grace from payment for welcome and salvation.

glossary.Restitution: Restitution means returning what was taken or compensating for a concrete loss where possible. It addresses material harm rather than merely the offender’s feeling of guilt.
glossary.Repentance: Repentance means turning from wrongdoing in attitude and conduct. In the guide’s account, it involves responsibility and genuine intent to change rather than payment for forgiveness.
glossary.Boundary: A boundary is a limit that can protect people. Considering forgiveness does not automatically remove a protective limit or restore trust.

metadata.deeper: Read the full encounter before treating one statement as a universal formula. Distinguish forgiveness, repaired material loss, and rebuilt trust; these are related but not identical.

sections.title: After forgiveness: love takes practical form

units.text: Grace and practical repair belong together, but making amends does not buy welcome or salvation.
Luke's encounter with Zacchaeus unfolds through seeking, meeting Jesus, welcome, complaint, and concern about possessions and wrongdoing.
Read this sequence before treating a statement about money as an abstract formula.
Jesus' approach and the crowd's objection belong to the story's meaning.
Our task is to distinguish a response to grace from a payment that supposedly makes God willing to save.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: Then Jesus entered Jericho and was passing through. And there was a man named Zacchaeus, a chief tax collector, who was very wealthy. He was trying to see who Jesus was, but could not see over the crowd because he was small in stature. So he ran on ahead and climbed a sycamore tree to see Him, since Jesus was about to pass that way. When Jesus came to that place, He looked up and said, “Zacchaeus, hurry down, for I must stay at your house today.” So Zacchaeus hurried down and welcomed Him joyfully. And all who saw this began to grumble, saying, “He has gone to be the guest of a sinful man!” But Zacchaeus stood up and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I give to the poor, and if I have cheated anyone, I will repay it fourfold.” Jesus said to him, “Today salvation has come to this house, because this man too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.”

displayLines: Luke 19:1–10 · BSB
Then Jesus entered Jericho and…

units.text: Zacchaeus speaks about giving and repayment.
Readers debate the statement's tense and implications, but its ethical concern is evident: money and the effects of wrongdoing matter in this encounter.
A religious experience cannot be detached from the neighbors affected by one's conduct.
Restitution means returning what was taken or compensating for a concrete loss where possible.
The guide treats repair as a response to grace.
Acknowledging the people harmed makes repentance more credible, because wrongdoing has consequences beyond the offender's feelings.
Forgiveness, however, does not entitle an offender to demand immediate trust or unrestricted access to the person injured.
Trust concerns whether someone can safely be relied upon; it need not be restored merely because forgiveness is being considered.

Canonical Shelf's own account of repentance has four parts: recognizing that an action contradicted God's loving purpose, taking responsibility without deflection or self-condemnation, apologizing, and genuinely intending a different outcome.
Whether the later change succeeds is not what makes the repentance genuine.
Asking for forgiveness can express repentance and relationship, but does not make God willing to forgive.
Shame can prevent a person from asking; Love does not withhold forgiveness because a wounded person cannot find the right words.
This is the guide's stated account, distinguished from what the narrative alone establishes.
Practical repair can include admission, restitution where possible, changed habits, and respect for boundaries that protect others.
Different harms call for different responses, so an apology is not a universal remedy for every loss.
Forgiveness, repaired material harm, and rebuilt trust are connected but distinct.
The lesson establishes a theological relationship between grace and conduct; it does not promise that every damaged relationship can be restored on demand.
Carry this distinction into the reflection: an apology should attend to the affected person's needs, rather than making their immediate trust a condition of the offender's willingness to change.

lessons.title: Cross, resurrection, and the gift of grace

metadata.title: Cross, resurrection, and the gift of grace
metadata.objective: Distinguish Christ’s saving work, receiving grace, and the response of discipleship.

glossary.Atonement: Atonement names Christ’s saving work in addressing sin and reconciliation with God. Christians describe that work through several images rather than one exhaustive picture.
glossary.Reconciliation: Reconciliation means restoring a relationship across estrangement or rupture. In these lessons, it concerns God’s saving work through Christ rather than a restoration humanity first achieves unaided.
glossary.Penal substitution: Penal substitution is an account of atonement in which Christ bears the penalty due to sinners. The guide accommodates this account without presenting it as the only scriptural explanation.

metadata.deeper: Compare the language of reconciliation in 2 Corinthians with victory in Colossians. What does each image illuminate, and what questions does it leave open?

sections.title: Cross, resurrection, and the gift of grace

units.text: Christian proclamation holds Jesus' death and resurrection together.
Paul recalls that Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised, and appeared to witnesses.
This is a proclamation about saving work, not only admiration for a kind person.
Humanity is not presented as accomplishing that saving work for itself.
We will distinguish what Christ accomplishes, how grace is received, and how discipleship responds, so that neither the gift nor the responsibility it invites disappears from the account.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: Now, brothers, I want to remind you of the gospel I preached to you, which you received, and in which you stand firm. By this gospel you are saved, if you hold firmly to the word I preached to you. Otherwise, you have believed in vain. For what I received I passed on to you as of first importance: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve. After that, He appeared to more than five hundred brothers at once, most of whom are still living, though some have fallen asleep. Then He appeared to James, then to all the apostles. And last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth.

displayLines: 1 Corinthians 15:1–8 · BSB
Now, brothers, I want to remind…

units.text: The guide teaches that sin separates humanity from God and brings humanity under judgment.
Through his willing sacrifice and resurrection, Jesus bears our sins, confronts their consequences, defeats sin and death, and makes reconciliation with God possible.
Reconciliation means restoring a ruptured relationship.
These are connected theological claims about the significance of Christ's work, and the New Testament expresses them through several themes rather than one exhaustive picture.
Penal substitution describes Christ as bearing the penalty due to sinners.
Other accounts emphasize victory over sin and death, sacrifice, representation, healing, and reconciliation.
The themes can overlap because they illuminate different dimensions of salvation.
Canonical Shelf accommodates penal substitution without making its particular account of punishment the sole explanation.
Paul's sequence in the reading identifies the proclaimed events; it does not by itself select one exclusive mechanism of atonement.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, made possible through Christ's sacrifice and resurrection.
In this guide, people receive it by acknowledging sin and their inability to save themselves, repenting, and trusting Christ's saving work.
Repentance and faith describe reception rather than achievement that establishes a debt owed by God.
Inability to merit salvation does not mean a person lacks value in God's eyes.
Ephesians connects grace with good works while denying grounds for boasting.
Loving action therefore belongs to the response to grace rather than the price of admission.
This order gives us a way to avoid two distortions: turning salvation into a merit contest, and reducing faith to words without responsibility.
Return to the three questions as you explain the lesson.
What does Christ accomplish?
How is the gift received?
What shape does the response take?
Distinguishing them makes their relationship clearer rather than separating grace from life.

lessons.title: Providence: purpose without erasing response

metadata.title: Providence: purpose without erasing response
metadata.objective: Distinguish providence, foreknowledge, and determinism within the guide’s account of meaningful response.

glossary.Providence: Providence means God’s care and purposes within the world and history. A claim about divine purpose does not itself establish that every harmful act is good.
glossary.Foreknowledge: Foreknowledge means knowing beforehand. Knowing and causing are distinct claims, which Christian systems relate in different ways.
glossary.Determinism: Determinism is an account in which events are determined by prior causes or conditions. It concerns what determines an event rather than simply whether it is known beforehand.

metadata.deeper: Compare the passage’s stated purpose with the outcomes readers sometimes promise on its behalf. It does not guarantee that every personal preference will be fulfilled.

units.text: Providence means God's care and purposes within the world and history.
Romans places that care within weakness and hope, beginning with the Spirit's intercession rather than with humans understanding every event.
Divine involvement is described in lives that remain limited and vulnerable.
We will distinguish knowing, causing, and bringing good from an event, because those are different claims with different consequences for hope and responsibility.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: In the same way, the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know how we ought to pray, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groans too deep for words. And He who searches our hearts knows the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God. And we know that God works all things together for the good of those who love Him, who are called according to His purpose. For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers. And those He predestined, He also called; those He called, He also justified; those He justified, He also glorified.

displayLines: Romans 8:26–30 · BSB
In the same way, the Spirit helps…

units.text: The statement about God working for good does not say that every harmful action is morally good.
The language that follows relates God's purpose to conformity to the Son.
Bringing good from cruelty therefore cannot be used to call cruelty necessary or desirable.
The promise concerns divine purpose; it does not remove the need to evaluate an actor's conduct.
Foreknowledge means knowing beforehand.
Predestination concerns an appointed end, and determinism concerns what determines events.
Christians relate these concepts differently, so the terms should not be treated as interchangeable definitions.
This guide affirms meaningful acceptance or resistance to grace while teaching that human choices cannot ultimately thwart God's purpose.
Canonical Shelf's own position is that God perfectly knows every possible choice and its consequences and perfectly understands every person.
A genuinely free choice is not a settled fact until the person makes it.
God influences, guides, and prepares circumstances without controlling the response, and that influence can be resisted.
Many Christian traditions instead hold that God knows every future choice in advance; some also hold that God determines it.
These views must be described accurately alongside the guide's own account rather than collapsed into one claim.
Even an account that affirms knowledge of an outcome still needs to explain whether and how it connects that knowledge with causation.
Knowing and causing are distinct claims.
Likewise, believing God can bring good from an event does not erase an actor's responsibility for harm.
These distinctions protect hope from becoming an excuse for cruelty.
Romans does not provide a complete philosophical model, guarantee every personal preference, or diagnose the reason for every tragedy.
The objective is to preserve both hope and responsibility: name harm honestly while allowing for healing and new good, without pretending the later good justifies the original action.

lessons.title: Speak carefully about God

metadata.title: Speak carefully about God
metadata.objective: Distinguish Trinity, incarnation, and providence while recognizing the limits of explanatory models.

glossary.Trinity: The Trinity is the historic Christian confession of one God in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. It preserves unity and real distinction rather than dividing God into three beings or parts.
glossary.Incarnation: Incarnation names the Christian claim that the Son became genuinely human in Jesus Christ. Historic teaching affirms full humanity and full divinity, rather than a disguise or mixture of incomplete halves.
glossary.Providence: Providence means God’s care and purposes within the world and history. A claim about divine purpose does not itself establish that every harmful act is good.

metadata.deeper: Compare what a biblical passage directly says with how a later doctrinal formulation draws several passages together. Both deserve careful study, but they are not identical literary acts.

units.text: Christian doctrine gathers and interprets biblical testimony through reasoned reflection.
Three recurring terms ask different questions: Trinity concerns who God is, incarnation concerns the Son becoming human, and providence concerns God's purposes in history.
The historic Trinity confesses one God in three persons, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
It affirms unity and real distinction together, so neither three independent gods nor one person merely changing roles states the teaching accurately.
Canonical Shelf also identifies its own governing convictions.
God is the loving Creator and source of all existence; God is Love and cannot act contrary to Love.
Created beings have genuine agency, so God does not determine every choice or directly cause every action.
This conviction about Love and freedom governs the guide's discussion of providence, forgiveness, judgment, and reconciliation.
Historic Christian formulations are taught alongside that position for religious literacy, without claiming that they all give the same account.

data.fullPassageText: Meanwhile, the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain Jesus had designated. When they saw Him, they worshiped Him, but some doubted. Then Jesus came to them and said, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me. Therefore go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey all that I have commanded you. And surely I am with you always, even to the end of the age.”

Meanwhile, the eleven disciples…

units.text: Incarnation names the Son's becoming human in Jesus Christ.
Historic Christianity confesses Jesus as fully divine and fully human.
A half-divine, half-human mixture would reduce both claims, so it does not explain the confession.
John's account of the Word and Philippians' account of self-giving provide primary readings with which to examine this language.
Begin with their testimony rather than treating the later doctrinal formulation as a quotation from either passage.
Teaching about the Spirit concerns life, prayer, community, and God's work among people.
Romans 8 describes divine help amid human weakness and hope.
That setting matters for discernment: understanding the Spirit does not require treating every intense feeling as a direct command from God.
Responsibility remains necessary when evaluating the claim and its effects on other people.
Providence concerns God's purposes and care within history.
The guide affirms meaningful human response: grace can be accepted or resisted, while human choices cannot ultimately thwart God's purpose.
Foreknowledge means knowing beforehand; predestination concerns an appointed outcome; determinism concerns how events are determined.
The concepts are related differently in different systems, but their meanings cannot simply be exchanged.
Analogies should be evaluated by the claims they explain.
Water changing states can obscure the distinction of persons, while dividing an object into thirds can imply that each person is only part of God.
State the doctrine, identify the feature an analogy illuminates, and acknowledge where it fails.
Mystery makes room for the limits of explanation without excusing careless reasoning.
The objective is to distinguish these questions and represent their answers accurately; participation does not require personal assent.

lessons.title: Incarnation: fully divine and fully human

metadata.title: Incarnation: fully divine and fully human
metadata.objective: Explain incarnation without reducing Jesus to a divine disguise or a half-human mixture.

glossary.Incarnation: Incarnation names the Christian claim that the Son became genuinely human in Jesus Christ. Historic teaching affirms full humanity and full divinity, rather than a disguise or mixture of incomplete halves.
glossary.Revelation: Revelation means making known what would otherwise remain hidden. John connects Jesus with making God known as well as with grace and truth.
glossary.Nature: Nature here concerns what is meant by being divine or human. Historic incarnation teaching does not treat either as an incomplete ingredient.

metadata.deeper: Distinguish what John explicitly narrates from later terminology used to synthesize it. An explanation should preserve the passage’s claims without pretending to settle every philosophical question.

sections.title: Incarnation: fully divine and fully human

units.text: Incarnation means the Son's becoming human in Jesus Christ.
John's opening places the Word in relation to God and then speaks of the Word becoming flesh.
The movement holds divine identity together with embodied life.
Our objective is to explain why the historic confession preserves both full divinity and full humanity.
Calling flesh an irrelevant outer costume would remove the embodied reality that John's language brings into the account.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was with God in the beginning. Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made. In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. The Light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There came a man who was sent from God. His name was John. He came as a witness to testify about the Light, so that through him everyone might believe. He himself was not the Light, but he came to testify about the Light. The true Light, who gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and though the world was made through Him, the world did not recognize Him. He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. But to all who did receive Him, to those who believed in His name, He gave the right to become children of God— children born not of blood, nor of the desire or will of man, but born of God. The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory, the glory of the one and only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth. John testified concerning Him. He cried out, saying, “This is He of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me has surpassed me because He was before me.’” From His fullness we have all received grace upon grace. For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.

displayLines: John 1:1–18 · BSB
In the beginning was the Word,…

units.text: Historic Christianity confesses Jesus as fully divine and fully human.
It does not describe two incomplete halves combining into an unusual third kind of being.
Each half would lack something the confession expressly affirms.
Nor is human life merely a visible performance without genuine human experience; such an explanation preserves appearance while losing the reality of humanity.
John also links Jesus with grace, truth, and making God known.
Revelation means making known what would otherwise remain hidden.
Incarnation therefore concerns revelation as well as presence: Christians look to Jesus to understand God's character.
The course reads human life, suffering, and self-giving in light of this confession, because genuine humanity cannot be discarded whenever its consequences become difficult to explain.
Compare John's presentation with Philippians 2:5–11.
Ask what each emphasizes before drawing the accounts into a summary.
John's explicit language and the later vocabulary of incarnation are related, but they are different literary acts.
A disciplined explanation keeps humanity and divinity in view instead of using one to cancel the other.
It can acknowledge philosophical questions it has not settled while still identifying why a disguise or a mixture fails to preserve the claim.
Return to that distinction as you explain the lesson: does the account maintain genuine human life as well as divine identity?

lessons.title: Christian practice: beliefs take a communal form

metadata.title: Christian practice: beliefs take a communal form
metadata.objective: Recognize worship, baptism, Communion, prayer, formation, generosity, and community as practices connected with Christian belief.

glossary.Baptism: Baptism is the Christian water rite associated with initiation and life in Christ. Romans 6 connects it with Christ’s death and a changed life, while traditions differ over its timing and relation to grace.
glossary.Communion: Communion is the Christian shared meal also called Eucharist or the Lord’s Supper. Traditions differ over its meaning and admission requirements.
glossary.Formation: Formation is the shaping of habits, understanding, and character through practices and relationships. Christian formation is communal as well as individual.

metadata.deeper: Acts summarizes one community at one moment. Description is not automatically prescription. The passage can still reveal priorities and relationships that later communities must reason about rather than mechanically copy.

drawers.title: Why communities differ
drawers.body: Sacramental theology, church governance, culture, history, and different interpretations of Scripture all shape Christian practice. Course 6 compares those differences directly.

sections.title: Christian practice: beliefs take a communal form

units.text: Christian beliefs take shape in worship, prayer, baptism, Communion, care, and communal life.
Christianity therefore involves more than agreeing with propositions.
The New Testament depicts people learning, praying, sharing meals, caring for needs, baptizing, remembering Jesus, worshiping, and making ethical decisions together.
These practices give belief a social and embodied form.
Our objective is to recognize their different purposes and the connections between what a community teaches and how it lives.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. A sense of awe came over everyone, and the apostles performed many wonders and signs. All the believers were together and had everything in common. Selling their possessions and goods, they shared with anyone who was in need. With one accord they continued to meet daily in the temple courts and to break bread from house to house, sharing their meals with gladness and sincerity of heart, praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.

displayLines: Acts 2:42–47 · BSB
They devoted themselves to the…

units.text: Acts 2 offers an idealized summary of an early Jerusalem community.
Teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, prayer, shared resources, and public life appear together.
This arrangement shows that Christian formation—the shaping of habits, understanding, and character—involves relationships as well as individual learning.
The summary describes a community at a particular moment; it is not a complete rulebook for every later congregation.
Baptism is the Christian water rite associated with initiation and life in Christ.
Communion, also called Eucharist or the Lord's Supper, is the Christian shared meal.
Traditions differ over the timing, meaning, admission, and relation to grace of these practices.
Prayer likewise extends beyond requests.
Praise, lament, confession, thanksgiving, intercession, and attentive listening all belong within Christian practice.
Distinguishing their purposes helps us avoid treating every practice as the same kind of action.
This lesson introduces a landscape in which baptism, Communion, prayer, ethics, worship, ministry, and denominational differences can be examined more closely.
A local practice cannot be assumed to represent every Christian community.
Sacramental theology, governance, culture, history, and interpretation all help explain variation.
Acts can reveal priorities and relationships without requiring mechanical reproduction of every economic arrangement.
The question to retain is how a practice gives communal form to belief, and what further evidence is needed before making it a universal requirement.

lessons.title: Baptism: sign, participation, and community

metadata.title: Baptism: sign, participation, and community
metadata.objective: Explain baptism’s connection with Christ and fairly distinguish infant and believer practices.

glossary.Baptism: Baptism is the Christian water rite associated with initiation and life in Christ. Romans 6 connects it with Christ’s death and a changed life, while traditions differ over its timing and relation to grace.
glossary.Profession of faith: A profession of faith is a person’s expressed confession or affirmation of faith. Believer-baptizing communities particularly emphasize this personal expression.
glossary.Sacramental: Sacramental describes a practice understood as a means or sign of God’s gracious action. Its precise meaning differs among Christian traditions.

metadata.deeper: Compare the theological meaning of baptism with its timing and ritual form. A shared word can conceal real differences that deserve fair explanation.

units.text: Baptism is the water rite associated with Christian initiation and life in Christ.
In Romans 6, Paul connects it with Christ's death and resurrection while arguing about a changed life.
That connection gives baptism more significance than an arbitrary membership badge: it locates the baptized person's identity in relation to Christ.
We will explain this connection while distinguishing the reasons churches give for infant and believer baptism.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase? Certainly not! How can we who died to sin live in it any longer? Or aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death? We were therefore buried with Him through baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may walk in newness of life.

displayLines: Romans 6:1–4 · BSB
What then shall we say? Shall we…

units.text: Christians disagree about how baptism relates to grace, faith, and salvation.
Some emphasize sacramental participation, describing the practice as a means or sign of God's gracious action.
Others emphasize the person's confession of faith and symbolic testimony.
The guide teaches baptism's spiritual and communal significance without declaring it a necessary condition for salvation.
A shared term therefore does not establish that all churches explain its action identically.
Infant-baptizing communities commonly emphasize divine initiative and nurture within the community.
Believer-baptizing communities emphasize the person's own profession of faith, meaning an expressed confession or affirmation.
These are different accounts of timing and practice, not proof that one side values faith and the other disregards it.
Fair comparison explains each rationale in terms its adherents recognize before evaluating its argument.
The connection with new life raises practical questions about continuing belonging.
Ask what promises are spoken, what responsibility the community undertakes, and how the practice is understood locally.
Those details make a conversation with a church more informed than a label alone can.
Neither this comparison nor the course should become a test that excludes a learner from welcome.
Our objective is to understand baptism's relation to Christ and the community while recognizing that this short passage does not settle every disagreement over timing or ritual form.

lessons.title: Put understanding into practice

metadata.title: Put understanding into practice
metadata.objective: Read a parable in context and connect mercy with concrete action.

glossary.Parable: A parable is a story used to provoke insight and response. In Luke 10, the story redirects a question about who counts as a neighbor toward practicing mercy.
glossary.Mercy: Mercy is compassion expressed through care for someone in need. The Samaritan’s response gives it practical form through tending wounds and arranging continuing care.
glossary.Grace: Grace means God’s freely given favor and saving gift. The guide distinguishes receiving that gift from earning it through achievements.

metadata.deeper: Christian traditions relate faith, justification, and works differently. Explain their reasoning fairly. In this guide, good works do not purchase salvation; love takes practical shape in response to grace.

units.text: A parable is a story that invites an audience to recognize, question, or reconsider something.
In Luke's conversation, a legal expert asks about eternal life and then asks who counts as a neighbor.
Jesus answers with the story of an assaulted traveler left injured.
The Samaritan becomes a neighbor by giving concrete care across a social boundary.
Our task is to see how the story redirects the question of who deserves mercy toward the action of practicing it.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: One day an expert in the law stood up to test Him. “Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” “What is written in the Law?” Jesus replied. “How do you read it?” He answered, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’ and ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ ” “You have answered correctly,” Jesus said. “Do this and you will live.” But wanting to justify himself, he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” Jesus took up this question and said, “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho when he fell into the hands of robbers. They stripped him, beat him, and went away, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down the same road, but when he saw him, he passed by on the other side. So too, when a Levite came to that spot and saw him, he passed by on the other side. But a Samaritan on a journey came upon him, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and took care of him. The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. ‘Take care of him,’ he said, ‘and on my return I will repay you for any additional expense.’ Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?” “The one who showed him mercy,” replied the expert in the law. Then Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.”

displayLines: Luke 10:25–37 · BSB
One day an expert in the law…

units.text: The story names a priest, a Levite, and a Samaritan.
Giving the Samaritan this role unsettles expectations across a real social and religious boundary.
The passage does not tell us every motive of the people who pass by, so a confident explanation of their reasons would add something the story has not supplied.
We can examine the actions it describes without pretending to know those motives.
Mercy takes practical form as the Samaritan approaches the injured person, tends wounds, transports him, arranges continuing care, and pays for it.
These actions show why loving intentions alone do not exhaust the account.
Jesus turns attention from identifying a category of acceptable neighbors toward becoming a neighbor through care.
The social boundary does not prevent the response, and the response continues beyond noticing the need.
Canonical Shelf teaches forgiveness and salvation as gifts of God's Love through Christ's sacrifice and resurrection.
They are received rather than earned, not rewards for deeds, rituals, or prescribed words.
Faith and repentance respond to the gift rather than paying for it.
The parable nevertheless gives discipleship concrete ethical content: mercy involves action and continuing responsibility.
Holding grace and conduct together prevents Christianity from becoming either a merit contest or words without consequences.
In the scenario that follows, the aim is to recognize actual need, cross the boundary, and follow through, rather than use care to demonstrate moral superiority.

lessons.title: One faith, many Christian traditions

metadata.title: One faith, many Christian traditions
metadata.objective: Distinguish shared Christian identity from real differences among traditions and learn a fair method for comparison.

glossary.Tradition: A tradition is a historically developed community of belief, worship, interpretation, and practice. The term can also refer to teaching and practice handed on within a community.
glossary.Denomination: A denomination is an organized Christian body or family with a shared identity and governance. Its name does not completely describe every congregation’s practice.
glossary.Ecumenism: Ecumenism is work toward understanding, relationship, cooperation, or unity among Christians across traditions. It need not erase their actual disagreements.

metadata.deeper: Internal diversity matters. National denominational documents, theological traditions, clergy, and individual congregations may not speak with one voice on every question.

drawers.title: What Canonical Shelf will compare
drawers.body: Authority, baptism, Communion, polity, worship, ministry, LGBTQ participation, theological emphases, and the relationship between official teaching and local practice.

drawers.title: Why 1 Corinthians 12?
drawers.body: Paul’s body imagery is not a modern denominational theory. It does supply a vocabulary of unity-with-difference that can help frame comparison without pretending every disagreement is trivial.

units.text: A Christian tradition is a historically developed community of belief, worship, interpretation, and practice.
Christians share Scripture, Jesus-centered confession, baptismal and worship traditions, and a history of common creeds as well as disagreements.
Christianity therefore names substantial common ground and communities that do not answer every question identically.
Our objective is to compare both realities through a tradition's own claims and actual practices rather than through stereotypes.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: There are different gifts, but the same Spirit. There are different ministries, but the same Lord. There are different ways of working, but the same God works all things in all people. Now to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good. To one there is given through the Spirit the message of wisdom, to another the message of knowledge by the same Spirit, to another faith by the same Spirit, to another gifts of healing by that one Spirit, to another the working of miracles, to another prophecy, to another distinguishing between spirits, to another speaking in various tongues, and to still another the interpretation of tongues. All these are the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines. The body is a unit, though it is composed of many parts. And although its parts are many, they all form one body. So it is with Christ. For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free, and we were all given one Spirit to drink.

displayLines: 1 Corinthians 12:4–13 · BSB
There are different gifts, but…

units.text: Differences concern authority, sacraments, church governance, ministry, salvation language, worship, biblical interpretation, sexuality, social ethics, and other questions.
Names such as Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, evangelical, mainline, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist, Baptist, Pentecostal, and Restorationist identify histories and families.
They cannot completely describe every congregation belonging to those families.
Fair comparison begins with a tradition's own sources.
Distinguish official teaching from local practice and describe disagreement in terms adherents would recognize.
A national statement can establish a body's stated policy; a local policy establishes what a congregation says it practices; one person's experience establishes something about that experience.
Treating any one of these as complete evidence for the others exaggerates what it can show.
A stronger comparison names actual differences while also noticing where a stereotype overstates them.
Canonical Shelf states its own editorial commitments while distinguishing text, evidence, interpretation, doctrine, reception, and application.
The deeper comparison of traditions continues that method.
Paul's body imagery in 1 Corinthians supplies a vocabulary of unity with difference, but it is not a theory of modern denominations or proof that all disagreements are trivial.
Ecumenism seeks understanding, cooperation, or unity across traditions.
The question that guides this work is how to identify real disagreement at the appropriate level of evidence without erasing common ground or internal diversity.

metadata.title: Seven traditions: compare claims and local practice
metadata.objective: Use a fair comparison method for the five traditions considered in this course.

glossary.Denomination: A denomination is an organized Christian body or family with a shared identity and governance. Its name does not completely describe every congregation’s practice.
glossary.Congregational life: Congregational life means the worship, decisions, and practices of a local community. Wider identity and official policy do not automatically establish all its local practices.
glossary.Sanctification: Sanctification means growth in holiness and transformed life. Traditions explain it differently, and Methodist teaching gives it particular emphasis.

metadata.deeper: Receiving others in Romans 14 should not be used to erase harmful conduct or all doctrinal distinctions. Identify what the ancient dispute is before drawing a modern comparison.

sections.title: Seven traditions: compare claims and local practice

units.text: This lesson considers five traditions: ELCA Lutheran, United Church of Christ, United Methodist, Episcopal, and Alliance of Baptists.
The aim is to compare official belief, local practice, and the questions that matter in an actual congregation.
These traditions are not interchangeable.
A national statement cannot automatically describe every local practice, and a denominational label begins an inquiry rather than completing it.
Read Romans 14 with that distinction in mind, while first identifying the differing practices addressed in Paul's own setting.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions. For one person has faith to eat all things, while another, who is weak, eats only vegetables. The one who eats everything must not belittle the one who does not, and the one who does not eat everything must not judge the one who does, for God has accepted him. Who are you to judge someone else’s servant? To his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand. One person regards a certain day above the others, while someone else considers every day alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind. He who observes a special day does so to the Lord; he who eats does so to the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and he who abstains does so to the Lord and gives thanks to God.

displayLines: Romans 14:1–6 · BSB
Accept him whose faith is weak,…

units.text: ELCA teaching gives particular attention to justification and law and gospel.
Methodist teaching emphasizes grace and sanctification, or growth in holiness and transformed life.
Episcopal identity includes Anglican worship and a tradition of common prayer.
These are starting emphases rather than exclusive possessions; each community also speaks about Scripture, discipleship, and shared life.
An emphasis can help orient comparison without defining everything a tradition believes.
United Church of Christ and Alliance communities give significant room to local congregational life while relating through wider structures.
Shared terms such as welcome and inclusion therefore require specific questions.
What does an official statement commit a congregation to, and how much room do local congregations have to differ?
Examine the statements rather than turning an emphasis into a stereotype.
The distinction between wider identity and local practice explains why a warm general description may leave important questions unanswered.
Canonical Shelf is explicitly LGBTQ-affirming and open-table, grounded in its own Statement of Faith rather than any one of these traditions.
Romans 14 teaches receiving others without treating every difference as grounds for contempt.
It does not settle every modern controversy, erase harmful conduct, or remove doctrinal distinctions.
Ask a local congregation about welcome, leadership, sacraments, and the handling of questions.
Specific answers about participation give practical meaning to a general claim.
The objective is an informed comparison, not an assumption that every tradition or every local community practices welcome identically.
