lessons.title: Covenant frameworks: continuity without erasing Israel

metadata.title: Covenant frameworks: continuity without erasing Israel
metadata.objective: Compare major Christian ways of relating biblical covenants, Israel, Church, and fulfillment while rejecting simplistic supersessionism.

glossary.Covenant Theology: Covenant theology is a family of Christian systems emphasizing covenantal continuity across Scripture. Forms vary, including how they organize theological covenants such as works and grace.
glossary.Dispensationalism: Dispensationalism is a family of systems emphasizing distinct administrations in biblical history. Its forms vary and often develop distinctive accounts of Israel, the Church, and prophecy.
glossary.Supersessionism: Supersessionism names a range of claims that the Church supersedes or replaces Israel. The term requires definition because its theological forms and uses vary.

metadata.deeper: “Supersessionism” is used broadly in scholarship and theology, so accusations require definition. Some Christian traditions affirm fulfillment in Christ while explicitly rejecting the idea that God has abandoned Jewish people or that the Church may treat Judaism with contempt.

drawers.title: Why Romans 11 matters
drawers.body: Paul’s olive-tree image includes warning to Gentile believers not to boast over branches. Whatever larger system one adopts, that warning constrains triumphalist application.

sections.title: Covenant frameworks: continuity without erasing Israel

units.text: Earlier study traced Noahic, Abrahamic, Sinai, Davidic, and new-covenant trajectories in biblical history.
Christian theology then asks how those covenants relate and how the Church relates to Israel.
A framework organizes answers to those questions, but different frameworks emphasize different relationships.
Our objective is to compare them while retaining the texts and rejecting Gentile superiority.
Romans 11 is consequential here because its olive-tree image warns Gentile believers against boasting over the branches.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: Now if some branches have been broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, have been grafted in among the others to share in the nourishment of the olive root, do not boast over those branches. If you do, remember this: You do not support the root, but the root supports you. You will say then, “Branches were broken off so that I could be grafted in.” That is correct: They were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but be afraid. For if God did not spare the natural branches, He will certainly not spare you either. Take notice, therefore, of the kindness and severity of God: severity to those who fell, but kindness to you, if you continue in His kindness. Otherwise you also will be cut off. And if they do not persist in unbelief, they will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again. For if you were cut from a wild olive tree, and contrary to nature were grafted into one that is cultivated, how much more readily will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree! I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, so that you will not be conceited: A hardening in part has come to Israel, until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. And so all Israel will be saved, as it is written: “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob. And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins.” Regarding the gospel, they are enemies on your account; but regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs. For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable.

units.text: Covenant theology is a family of systems that commonly emphasizes continuity across God's covenantal purposes.
It often organizes Scripture through theological covenants such as works and grace, with important variation among Reformed and other traditions.
Dispensationalism is another family, generally making sharper distinctions between administrations in biblical history and often maintaining a distinctive future role for ethnic or national Israel.
These broad descriptions orient a comparison rather than eliminating variation within either family.
Other traditions reject both systems or use different categories.
Romans 9–11 remains central because Paul speaks about Gentile inclusion, Israel, divine faithfulness, warning against Gentile boasting, and unresolved mystery together.
A framework that explains only one of those concerns still has to account for the others.
Its organizing categories do not replace the connected argument of the text.
Supersessionism names a range of claims that the Church supersedes or replaces Israel, so the term requires definition before it can evaluate a particular position.
A claim about fulfillment in Christ does not automatically prove that God abandoned Jewish people.
Canonical Shelf rejects the idea that Christian belonging permits contempt for Jews or establishes such abandonment.
A responsible framework must account for the actual texts and the ethical consequences of its language about Israel and Judaism.
The warning against boasting constrains application even where Christians continue to disagree about the larger system.

metadata.title: Understand Christian differences without caricature
metadata.objective: Compare shared Christian claims and differing structures while identifying this guide’s own commitments.

glossary.Creed: A creed is a shared, concise formulation of central beliefs. It gathers an interpretation of Scripture rather than replacing the need to read and examine it.
glossary.Ecumenism: Ecumenism is work toward understanding, relationship, cooperation, or unity among Christians across traditions. It need not erase their actual disagreements.
glossary.Polity: Polity means a church’s structure of organization and governance. Knowing who makes decisions does not by itself establish what doctrines they will affirm.

metadata.deeper: Compare a denomination’s official statement with a local congregation’s practice. Neither should automatically be treated as a complete description of the other.

units.text: Christian traditions share texts and central claims while differing about authority and practice.
A creed is a concise formulation of foundational belief; confessions and other statements can articulate further teaching.
Historical divisions involve theology, authority, worship, culture, and institutions, so one label rarely explains every congregation or person.
We will compare shared claims and differing structures while openly identifying the guide's commitments.
Fair comparison requires learning the reasons people give, not merely the descriptions their critics supply.

units.text: Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant traditions relate Scripture, inherited tradition, and church authority differently.
Their understandings of ministry and sacraments also vary.
Polity means the structure of church governance: some organize through bishops, others through councils of elders, and others emphasize congregational autonomy.
These structures provide starting points for comparison rather than a ranking of the sincerity of their members.
The Reformation and other reform movements raised questions about authority, grace, faith, and church life.
Protestant traditions also differ internally.
Lutheran teaching emphasizes justification and law and gospel, Wesleyan teaching emphasizes grace and sanctification, and Baptist traditions emphasize religious liberty and local church freedom.
These descriptions identify emphases; they do not make each concern the exclusive possession of one group.
Official statements and local practices both matter, and neither completely describes the other.
Canonical Shelf is grounded in its own published Statement of Faith, rather than a denomination.
Its commitments include an open table, explicit LGBTQ affirmation, Christian unity, contextual reading, and freedom of inquiry.
It teaches historic doctrine substantively while making assent unnecessary for learning, and it does not claim to speak for any church or movement.
Ecumenism seeks Christian relationship and cooperation without pretending disagreement has disappeared.
A fair conversation asks what a tradition affirms, why adherents find the claim persuasive, and where it affects practice.
Accurate understanding does not oblige a learner to adopt the account.
The objective is to represent both common ground and actual difference, while keeping the guide's own standpoint visible.
That makes disagreement reviewable instead of disguising it through stereotypes or claims of neutrality.

The historic teaching about Trinity and incarnation belongs to this conversation.

A later phrase may seek to prevent a misunderstanding without appearing verbatim in the earlier biblical text.

It can also mark boundaries.
Christians differ over the authority of particular formulations.
This course does not require a learner to recite a creed as a personal profession: accurate understanding and personal assent are distinct outcomes.

glossary.Ecumenism: Ecumenism is work toward understanding, relationship, cooperation, or unity among Christians across traditions. It need not erase their actual disagreements.

sections.title: Authority and unity across Christian traditions

units.text: Ephesians calls for humility, patience, and efforts toward unity.
Its repeated language of one gives that unity a theological foundation in shared commitments.
Yet the passage is not a modern denominational directory and does not settle every later institutional disagreement.
We will compare sources of authority and forms of church life while distinguishing unity from identical customs.
The way Christians treat one another remains relevant even when they disagree about how a decision should be authorized.

Polity means church organization and governance.

Governance and doctrine are related but distinct: knowing who makes a decision does not establish what decision that person or body will make.

lessons.title: Difficult ethical texts: neither avoidance nor easy excuses

metadata.title: Difficult ethical texts: neither avoidance nor easy excuses
metadata.objective: Distinguish a text’s explicit appeal, historical setting, and unresolved ethical questions.

glossary.Historical context: Historical context means the circumstances in which a text and its audience are situated. Understanding those circumstances does not automatically justify the practices they include.
glossary.Ethical evaluation: Ethical evaluation is judgment about the rightness and effects of an action. It differs from explaining why the action occurred in a historical setting.
glossary.Interpretive limit: An interpretive limit is a boundary beyond which the available evidence does not settle a claim. Naming it distinguishes an explicit statement from a stronger inference.

metadata.deeper: Philemon’s appeal and modern abolition are not identical statements. Examine the relationship between them without claiming the letter explicitly answers every later question.

sections.title: Difficult ethical texts: neither avoidance nor easy excuses

units.text: Philemon requires us to examine both what Paul says and what remains unresolved.
Paul appeals concerning Onesimus through love, relationship, and reception as a brother.
Read that actual wording before substituting either a modern abolition statement or a defense of slavery.
Our objective is to distinguish the explicit appeal, its historical setting, and the ethical questions it raises.
Understanding the setting is necessary for interpretation, but it does not require excusing the harms found within it.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well. I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. I am sending back to you him who is my very heart. I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will. For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good— no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord. So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self. Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask.

displayLines: Philemon 1:8–21 · BSB
So although in Christ I am bold…

units.text: The letter operates in a world where slavery existed.
That fact helps explain the situation Paul addresses; it does not establish that slavery was morally acceptable.
Historical context explains circumstances, while ethical evaluation asks about an action's rightness and effects.
Treating the first as a complete answer to the second changes the kind of question rather than answering it.
Examine how the appeal presses for a changed relationship and what it leaves unstated.
Christians have used biblical texts in opposing ways concerning slavery, so the interpretive history is not uncomplicated.
A responsible account must confront the harm of oppressive uses.
It should also distinguish an implication drawn from Paul's language of brotherhood from something the letter states explicitly.
This allows the appeal's significance to be examined without claiming that it supplies an entire modern abolition platform.
Use this method with conquest and restrictions on women as well.
Record explicit claims, examine context and competing interpretations, name the moral problem, and evaluate application through Jesus' teaching and human dignity.
A desirable conclusion still needs a visible argument, and a common ancient practice still needs moral evaluation.
Some questions remain difficult after careful study.
Naming that limit is part of an honest reading: it keeps the text's actual appeal, proposed implications, and unresolved ethical concerns open to examination.

lessons.title: Stay honest with difficult questions

metadata.title: Stay honest with difficult questions
metadata.objective: Address suffering, difficult ethical texts, and religious difference with evidence and care.

glossary.Theodicy: Theodicy is an attempt to account for evil and suffering in relation to God’s goodness. Rejecting one explanation of suffering does not resolve every question in this discussion.
glossary.Interpretive boundary: An interpretive boundary marks the limit of what the available evidence establishes. It keeps an explanation from presenting uncertainty as knowledge.
glossary.Religious literacy: Religious literacy means understanding beliefs and practices accurately, including diversity within traditions. It requires more than recognizing a religious label.

metadata.deeper: For a difficult passage, list its explicit statements, your interpretation, the moral question, and the proposed application separately. This makes disagreement easier to examine without disguising it.

units.text: Questions about evil and suffering are intellectual and personal at the same time.
Luke 13 challenges the inference that victims suffered because they were worse sinners than others.
The guide distinguishes wrongdoing enabled by human freedom from disease and disasters within a dynamic natural world, while acknowledging that this does not explain why God permits every loss.
Our objective is to address suffering, difficult ethical texts, and religious difference through evidence and care.
Reading directly and admitting what remains unresolved protects inquiry from adding unsupported accusations to someone's pain.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: At that time some of those present told Jesus about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. To this He replied, “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans, because they suffered this way? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish. Or those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam collapsed on them: Do you think that they were more sinful than all the others living in Jerusalem? No, I tell you. But unless you repent, you too will all perish.”

displayLines: Luke 13:1–5 · BSB
At that time some of those…

units.text: God can bring healing and good from suffering without making the suffering good in itself or every tragedy a deliberate lesson.
Lament, uncertainty, practical help, and hope can therefore belong together.
Biblical miracles deserve serious study alongside differing interpretations, but neither a diagnosis nor an unhealed condition establishes possession or inadequate faith.
An account of God's action cannot simply be assumed from the fact of suffering.
Conquest, slavery, and restrictions on women likewise require direct examination.
In Philemon, study Paul's appeal to receive Onesimus as a brother while distinguishing the actual wording from what it leaves unresolved about slavery.
Historical context helps explain a situation; it does not automatically excuse harm or settle its moral evaluation.

metadata.title: Inclusion: explain disagreement without putting dignity on trial

glossary.Affirming: Affirming here means recognizing LGBTQ relationships, marriage, and equal participation in Christian community. Canonical Shelf states this as its own commitment rather than a consensus among Christians.
glossary.Scope: Scope means the range of conduct or people to which an argument or instruction applies. A proposed application needs reasons for extending the claim to that range.
glossary.Ethical principle: An ethical principle is a guiding concern used in reasoning about conduct. Love of God and neighbor guides this lesson without removing the need to interpret specific passages.

metadata.deeper: Love is not a shortcut that removes the need to interpret specific texts. A careful argument explains its textual reasoning and practical effects.

lessons.title: Jewish roots and respectful religious difference

metadata.title: Jewish roots and respectful religious difference
metadata.objective: Reject a simple abandonment account of Israel while distinguishing Christian witness from certainty about individuals.

glossary.Covenant: A covenant is a committed relationship involving divine promise and communal responsibility. Christians differ over how biblical covenants relate to Israel and the Church.
glossary.Remnant: A remnant is a remaining group within a wider people. The theme appears in several biblical settings and contributes to Paul’s argument about Israel.
glossary.Witness: Witness means communicating faith through words and conduct without claiming control over another’s response. Respectful witness includes listening and accurate description.

metadata.deeper: Read Romans 9–11 as a connected argument before using one sentence to settle every question about Israel. This lesson establishes a boundary against simplistic abandonment, not a complete covenant theory.

sections.title: Jewish roots and respectful religious difference

units.text: Paul asks whether God has rejected his people and answers no, identifying himself within Israel as part of the response.
That argument obstructs a simplistic story in which Christianity begins only after God discards Israel.
Our objective is to reject that abandonment account while distinguishing Christian witness from certainty about individuals.
Christianity's Jewish roots and continuing religious difference call for accurate description and respect, rather than an explanation that erases the community Paul is discussing.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: I ask then, did God reject His people? Certainly not! I am an Israelite myself, a descendant of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. God did not reject His people, whom He foreknew. Do you not know what the Scripture says about Elijah, how he appealed to God against Israel: “Lord, they have killed Your prophets and torn down Your altars. I am the only one left, and they are seeking my life as well” ? And what was the divine reply to him? “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” In the same way, at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace. And if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works. Otherwise, grace would no longer be grace.

displayLines: Romans 11:1–6 · BSB

units.text: Jesus, Paul, and the earliest Christian movement belong within Jewish history.
Judaism also continues as a living tradition with its own reading of Scripture.
It should not be described merely as a failed precursor whose only purpose was to prepare for someone else's religion.
Paul's response in Romans 11 belongs to a connected argument about Israel, so one sentence should not be made to settle every covenant question.
Christian teaching about salvation through Christ raises genuine questions about covenant and people of other faiths.
Christians answer differently.
The guide teaches Christ's saving significance without assigning a known final destiny to particular people or presenting speculation about repeated lives as doctrine.

Canonical Shelf's own position reads Jesus' words “no one comes to the Father except through me” in John 14:6 as meaning that reconciliation rests on what God revealed and accomplished through Jesus, rather than on a conscious Christian profession made in this life.
Many Christians read the verse as requiring that profession.
The guide names and teaches both interpretations from the text, distinguishing its own account from the alternative rather than claiming consensus.
Witness means communicating faith through words and conduct without claiming control of another person's response.
Respectful witness includes accurate description, listening, and rejection of collective Jewish blame for Jesus' death.
Disagreement about truth does not authorize contempt or replace a community's own account of itself.
Begin by learning what another person actually believes.
Romans 11 establishes a boundary against simplistic abandonment, not a complete covenant theory or knowledge of every person's destiny.
Carry that boundary into conversation by distinguishing the guide's teaching about salvation from claims about individuals it cannot responsibly make.

metadata.title: Suffering, miracles, and spiritual discernment
metadata.objective: Distinguish theological questions from unsupported judgments about victims or illness.

glossary.Moral evil: Moral evil means harm connected with wrongdoing and the use of human agency. The guide distinguishes it from suffering not attributed to a directly identified malicious act.
glossary.Natural suffering: Natural suffering means suffering connected with disease or natural events rather than a directly identified malicious act. The distinction does not explain why God permits every loss.
glossary.Theodicy: Theodicy is an attempt to account for evil and suffering in relation to God’s goodness. Rejecting one explanation of suffering does not resolve every question in this discussion.

metadata.deeper: The passage’s rejection of one inference does not answer every philosophical question. State both what it challenges and what remains unresolved.

units.text: Luke 13 addresses the inference that victims of particular tragedies were worse sinners than others.
Jesus challenges that judgment through examples of human violence and a falling tower.
The passage does not supply a complete theory of suffering, but it directly resists this way of blaming victims.

Care can begin before every question about God and suffering has been answered.

metadata.title: Complete an independent reading project
metadata.objective: Build and explain a contextual reading that distinguishes evidence, interpretation, disagreement, and application.

glossary.Evidence record: An evidence record gathers textual observations and sourced contextual information. It keeps explicit statements identifiable alongside reconstructions and unanswered questions.
glossary.Alternative interpretation: An alternative interpretation is another reasoned account of a passage’s meaning. A fair comparison explains why a reader could find it persuasive.
glossary.Synthesis: Synthesis is a connected explanation that brings observations and distinctions into a coherent account. Its reasoning should remain open to review and revision.

metadata.deeper: Read all of Jude after the selected ending. Compare the call to mercy with the letter’s warnings. How does the whole letter complicate a summary based only on its final blessing?

units.text: An introductory guide should eventually help you read with less dependence on the guide.

glossary.Book profile: A book profile records a book’s content, people, opening, authorial information, and audience. References and labeled uncertainties help separate observation from assumed background.
glossary.Observation: An observation is a statement about what the text actually presents. It should be distinguished from an inference about missing circumstances.
glossary.Reconstruction: A reconstruction is an account of missing context inferred from evidence. It should be labeled as an inference rather than presented as the text’s direct statement.

metadata.title: Project lab 3: explain, apply, and revisit
metadata.objective: Complete a five-part study brief and evaluate a proportionate application.

glossary.Synthesis: Synthesis is a connected explanation that brings observations and distinctions into a coherent account. Its reasoning should remain open to review and revision.
glossary.Proportionate application: A proportionate application is a response no broader or more certain than its reasons justify. It remains accountable to its effects on other people.
glossary.Retrieval practice: Retrieval practice means recalling material before checking and correcting it. Explaining a book without the first draft gives you something to compare with that draft.

metadata.deeper: The app checks the study method, not the quality of every private essay. A trusted discussion partner can supply feedback that an automated completion milestone cannot.

lessons.title: Apocalypse: symbols directed toward hope

metadata.title: Apocalypse: symbols directed toward hope
metadata.objective: Read renewed-creation imagery in relation to divine presence rather than headline prediction.

glossary.Apocalypse: An apocalypse is an unveiling conveyed through visionary and symbolic forms. Reading its images requires attention to their literary setting and purpose.
glossary.New creation: New creation names the renewal of life and creation within Christian final hope. Revelation joins this imagery with divine presence and the ending of suffering.
glossary.Allusion: An allusion is a reference or echo connecting a text with another passage or image. A returning image need not perform exactly the same role in its new setting.

metadata.deeper: The return of an image is a literary connection, not proof that every physical detail must be identical. Compare what each passage does with it.

units.text: An apocalypse is an unveiling conveyed through visionary and symbolic forms.
Revelation's vision describes a new heaven and earth and a city descending from God.
That direction resists an account in which hope consists only of leaving creation behind.
Renewed life is joined to God's dwelling among people.
Our objective is to read these images in relation to divine presence and the end of suffering before assigning them to a contemporary headline.

Revelation also includes messages to congregations, symbolic conflict, worship, and judgment.
These forms belong in the same reading, rather than being detached whenever a striking contemporary resemblance appears.
A comparison between a number or beast and a current personality does not itself establish the symbol's referent.
Its literary setting and the evidence for the connection still need examination.
Compare the tree of life in Revelation 22 with Genesis 3.
An allusion is an echo or reference connecting texts, and the returning image links beginnings with endings while its setting and function change.

lessons.title: Millennium and rapture: name the frameworks before debating them

metadata.title: Millennium and rapture: name the frameworks before debating them
metadata.objective: Distinguish major millennial frameworks and locate rapture/dispensational readings within Christian interpretive history without making one timeline the course’s doctrinal center.

glossary.Premillennialism: Premillennialism is a family of views placing Christ’s return before a future millennial reign. Historic and dispensational forms should not be treated as synonyms.
glossary.Amillennialism: Amillennialism reads Revelation’s millennium symbolically or as the present messianic reign. It does not treat it as a future earthly thousand-year phase.
glossary.Postmillennialism: Postmillennialism is a family of views expecting a long period of gospel-shaped flourishing before Christ’s return. Its sequence differs from premillennial accounts.
glossary.Dispensationalism: Dispensationalism is a family of systems emphasizing distinct administrations in biblical history. Its forms vary and often develop distinctive accounts of Israel, the Church, and prophecy.

metadata.deeper: Historical development matters. Modern dispensationalism emerges in the nineteenth century, while millennial debates are much older. “The early Church believed X” usually requires more precise evidence than popular end-times arguments provide.

drawers.title: Rapture vocabulary
drawers.body: The English word comes through Latin terminology for being “caught up.” Vocabulary does not settle whether the event is separate from or part of the public coming of Christ.

sections.title: Millennium and rapture: name the frameworks before debating them

units.text: Revelation 20 describes a thousand-year reign, and Christian interpreters organize that imagery in several ways.
Premillennial approaches place Christ's return before a future millennium.
Postmillennial approaches expect a period of gospel-shaped flourishing before Christ's return.
Amillennial approaches read the millennium symbolically or as the present reign of Christ and the saints rather than a future earthly thousand-year phase.
Our objective is to name these frameworks before debating them, while keeping their disputed sequences distinct from the broader Christian emphasis on resurrection and final hope.

lessons.title: Resurrection, judgment, and renewed creation

metadata.title: Resurrection, judgment, and renewed creation
metadata.objective: Distinguish resurrection and renewed creation from disputed end-times timelines and repeated earthly lives.

glossary.Resurrection: Resurrection means God’s raising of the dead to transformed life. It differs from reincarnation into repeated earthly lives.
glossary.Eschatology: Eschatology is the study of final hope, judgment, and the last things. It includes more than proposed schedules of final events.
glossary.Renewed creation: Renewed creation names the world’s restoration under God’s life-giving presence. The vision’s imagery should not be treated as a complete account of future physical mechanics.

metadata.deeper: Compare the tree-of-life imagery in Genesis and Revelation. Notice the narrative connection without assuming that every image defines the physical mechanics of the future.

units.text: Christian hope centers on resurrection and life with God.
Paul connects Christ's resurrection with the future of those who belong to him, describing death as an enemy to be overcome.
This concerns God's saving action, not a human technique for escaping mortality or a change of address that makes embodied life irrelevant.
Our objective is to distinguish resurrection and renewed-creation imagery from disputed schedules and repeated earthly lives, while retaining the questions Christians continue to debate.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: But Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead comes also through a man. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive. But each in his own turn: Christ the firstfruits; then at His coming, those who belong to Him. Then the end will come, when He hands over the kingdom to God the Father after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power. For He must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death. For “God has put everything under His feet.” Now when it says that everything has been put under Him, this clearly does not include the One who put everything under Him. And when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.

displayLines: 1 Corinthians 15:20–28 · BSB
But Christ has indeed been raised…

units.text: Elsewhere in Paul's resurrection argument, contrasts describe transformed embodied life.
A spiritual body should not automatically mean an immaterial ghost: the language compares conditions of embodied existence.
Christian traditions debate details, but bodily resurrection is the historic emphasis taught here.
The transformation does not require treating present bodily life as something that never mattered.
Revelation's visions culminate in renewed creation, divine presence, and the ending of death and tears.
The returning tree of life connects final hope with Genesis imagery.
These symbolic and apocalyptic forms require contextual interpretation rather than confident assignments of beasts, numbers, or catastrophe to each day's headlines.
A narrative connection illuminates meaning without specifying every physical mechanism of the future.
Judgment, salvation through Christ, and eternal life are substantive Christian teachings.
Christians disagree about the nature and duration of hell, the unevangelized, and detailed sequences of final events.
The guide explains principal arguments without claiming knowledge of particular individuals' destiny.
Resurrection differs from reincarnation or repeated earthly lives, which this curriculum does not teach.

Canonical Shelf's Statement of Faith holds that God's Love remains available after death: all will be raised, and the guide expects all eventually to be reconciled to God through genuine repentance and their own free choice.
That is its position rather than Christian consensus.
Many Christians instead understand a person's choice as final at death, and that account is also presented accurately.
The guide takes no definitive position on creation's final physical state.
Its practical emphasis is hope encouraging faithfulness, care, and justice now, rather than speculation that distracts from responsibility.

lessons.title: Resurrection: transformed life rather than escape

metadata.title: Resurrection: transformed life rather than escape
metadata.objective: Explain Paul’s continuity-and-transformation imagery without reducing resurrection to a ghostly existence.

glossary.Resurrection: Resurrection means God’s raising of the dead to transformed life. It differs from reincarnation into repeated earthly lives.
glossary.Imperishable: Imperishable means not subject to the decay described in Paul’s contrast. It is part of his explanation of transformed life.
glossary.Continuity: Continuity means a connection between what exists now and what is transformed. Paul’s seed image holds this connection together with change.

metadata.deeper: An image can illuminate transformation without explaining its mechanics. Ask which feature of the comparison serves Paul’s argument.

sections.title: Resurrection: transformed life rather than escape

units.text: Paul answers questions about how the dead are raised and what kind of body is involved.
His seed comparison holds continuity and transformation together: there is a connection between what exists now and what is changed.
The image helps explain the claim, but it does not supply a detailed biological mechanism for resurrection.
Our objective is to understand transformed embodied life without reducing it to ghostly existence or pressing every feature of an analogy into a future specification.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: But someone will ask, “How are the dead raised? With what kind of body will they come?” You fool! What you sow does not come to life unless it dies. And what you sow is not the body that will be, but just a seed, perhaps of wheat or something else. But God gives it a body as He has designed, and to each kind of seed He gives its own body. Not all flesh is the same: Men have one kind of flesh, animals have another, birds another, and fish another. There are also heavenly bodies and earthly bodies. But the splendor of the heavenly bodies is of one degree, and the splendor of the earthly bodies is of another. The sun has one degree of splendor, the moon another, and the stars another; and star differs from star in splendor. So will it be with the resurrection of the dead: What is sown is perishable; it is raised imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power. It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. If there is a natural body, there is also a spiritual body. So it is written: “The first man Adam became a living being”; the last Adam a life-giving spirit. The spiritual, however, was not first, but the natural, and then the spiritual. The first man was of the dust of the earth, the second man from heaven. As was the earthly man, so also are those who are of the earth; and as is the heavenly man, so also are those who are of heaven. And just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man.

lessons.title: Judgment: serious teaching with interpretive limits

metadata.title: Judgment: serious teaching with interpretive limits
metadata.objective: Take judgment and mercy seriously while distinguishing the text from certainty about particular people.

glossary.Judgment: Judgment means God’s evaluation of life and conduct. Taking it seriously does not give a reader complete knowledge of each person’s final destiny.
glossary.Universal reconciliation: Universal reconciliation is an interpretation expecting the eventual reconciliation of all. Canonical Shelf holds a form of this view while acknowledging that Christians dispute it.
glossary.Final destruction: Final destruction is an interpretation in which final punishment ends in destruction rather than endless conscious existence. It differs from both eternal conscious punishment and universal reconciliation.

metadata.deeper: Compare Matthew 25 with the grace passages in Unit 9. Explain how your reading relates them instead of letting one isolated formulation cancel the other.

sections.title: Judgment: serious teaching with interpretive limits

units.text: Matthew's scene presents judgment through a king's separation of groups and their treatment of people in need.
Its dramatic form gives conduct toward others serious weight.
Christian hope includes accountability as well as reassurance.
Our objective is to take judgment and mercy seriously while distinguishing interpretation of the passage from certainty about particular people's final destiny.
The scene challenges indifference without giving a reader complete knowledge of another person's relationship with God.

sections.title: Read the passage with the question in view

data.fullPassageText: When the Son of Man comes in His glory, and all the angels with Him, He will sit on His glorious throne. All the nations will be gathered before Him, and He will separate the people one from another, as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. He will place the sheep on His right and the goats on His left. Then the King will say to those on His right, ‘Come, you who are blessed by My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave Me something to eat, I was thirsty and you gave Me something to drink, I was a stranger and you took Me in, I was naked and you clothed Me, I was sick and you looked after Me, I was in prison and you visited Me.’ Then the righteous will answer Him, ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry and feed You, or thirsty and give You something to drink? When did we see You a stranger and take You in, or naked and clothe You? When did we see You sick or in prison and visit You?’ And the King will reply, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of Mine, you did for Me.’ Then He will say to those on His left, ‘Depart from Me, you who are cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave Me nothing to eat, I was thirsty and you gave Me nothing to drink, I was a stranger and you did not take Me in, I was naked and you did not clothe Me, I was sick and in prison and you did not look after Me.’ And they too will reply, ‘Lord, when did we see You hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to You?’ Then the King will answer, ‘Truly I tell you, whatever you did not do for one of the least of these, you did not do for Me.’ And they will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

units.text: The identity of the least of these and the passage's relationship to wider salvation teaching are debated.
State the reasons for a reading and compare it with other texts.
A judgment scene should not silently replace the whole account of grace with a score of good deeds.
Explain the relationship rather than letting one isolated formulation cancel the other.
Christians also disagree about final punishment.
Eternal conscious separation or punishment, final destruction, and universal reconciliation are distinct interpretations.
Final destruction understands punishment as ending in destruction rather than endless conscious existence; universal reconciliation expects the eventual reconciliation of all.
Their arguments draw on different passages and readings of key language.
Describing each view accurately does not make the course adopt all of them.
The guide teaches salvation through Christ and the seriousness of judgment without declaring particular individuals' destiny.
Its practical direction is attentive care, repentance, and hope.
Speculation about the future must not become a way to evade a need in front of us.
Canonical Shelf's Statement of Faith holds that Christ has already saved humanity from death, so all will be raised, while distinguishing resurrection from reconciliation.
At judgment, God reveals who God is and what God accomplished through Jesus; each person remains free to respond.
God knows the heart and recognizes genuine repentance and response rather than merely outward or coerced conduct.
The Statement expects all eventually to seek the Source of Love freely and genuinely and be reconciled, until evil itself ceases.
This is the guide's form of universal reconciliation, not a consensus.
Passages used for other views are also taught.
The distinction allows the guide's position to be explained without pretending that unresolved disagreement removes the scene's urgent challenge about treatment of others.
